papers.title: Analyzing the distributions of influential and susceptible members in a multi-agent model of text-based online communities
papers.abstract: Abstract The topic of influence has existed for millennia, as people have sought to convince, persuade, or coerce others into adopting a perspective or taking an action they would not have taken on their own. The internet has allowed influence practitioners to refine their craft in various ways, including through online social networks, online communities, and blogs. Typical studies of influence aim to identify the most influential community member but do not attempt to pinpoint those most susceptible to influence. In this work, we advocate exploring the distribution of both the probability of being influential and the probability of being susceptible to influence among members of text-based online communities. We employed an agent-based model of such communities to conduct our studies. We compared the distributions of the probability of being influential generated by our Influence Score algorithm with those produced by traditional Centrality and Link Analysis algorithms. Our findings revealed that our Influence Score algorithm produced a distribution that, at the 0.05 significance level, was like that produced by the Hubs Link Analysis algorithm. The other algorithms were shown, also at the 0.05 significance level, to be different. The distribution of the probability of being susceptible to influence showed very few members with probabilities matching those of the most susceptible, but indicated a greater likelihood that multiple members could be considered highly susceptible to influence. These results suggest areas for future research and present ideas for leaders or organizers of text-based online communities to consider as they contemplate how to protect their communities from influence schemes.

papers.title: Interpreting breakthrough infections given assortative mixing of partially vaccinated populations
papers.abstract: Abstract Declining vaccine coverage across the United States has increased the risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases. Even when vaccines have low primary failure rates, conventional epidemic theory predicts a strongly nonlinear, positive relationship between vaccine coverage and the fraction of breakthrough infections in vaccinated individuals. These breakthrough infections may generate misconceptions that vaccines are not working and accelerate declines in coverage. Here, test predictions of epidemic theory that assumes random mixing between individuals irrespective of vaccine status. In contrast to expectations from random mixing models, we find a far lower fraction of breakthrough infections in measles outbreak data from seven states in the United States. To explore this discrepancy, we evaluate an alternative, compartmental disease model that accounts for preferential mixing (‘assortativity’) between people with the same vaccination status. The model with assortativity predicts lower fractions of breakthrough infections, consistent with observations from measles outbreak data, even when accounting for potential underascertainment of breakthrough infections. Next, we leverage the deviation between statewide and school-level vaccine MMR coverage in sixteen states, finding substantial assortativity. Our model accounting for assortativity predicts the total number of breakthrough infections is nonlinear, peaking at intermediate coverage below vaccine-derived herd immunity. Nationally, more than 90% of counties that report MMR coverage are above the model-predicted breakthrough-maximizing coverage, suggesting that they are at risk for increasing breakthrough infections if coverage declines. Vaccination outreach and monitoring campaigns should develop proactive strategies to contextualize breakthrough infections before low levels of primary failure contributes to population-scale increases in preventable disease.
